title_ar: فضيلة الشيخ الددو يُحاضر لجمعية المستقبل تحت عنوان: "قل هذه سبيلي"
title_en: Sheikh al-Dedew Lectures to the Future Association under the Title "Say: This Is My Way"
body_ar: استضاف فضاء التنوع الثقافي مساء أمس الثلاثاء 04 جمادى الأولى 1433هـ الموافق: 27 مارس 2012 محاضرة علمية هامة نظمتها جمعية المستقبل تحت عنوان: "قل هذه سبيلي" وقد ألقى المحاضرة فضيلة الشيخ محمد الحسن ولد الددو رئيس مركز تكوين العلماء ورئيس جمعية المستقبل للدعوة والثقافة والتعليم، وسط إقبال جماهيري كثيف غصت به جنبات الفضاء الواسع. وفي مستهل حديثه تحدث فضيلة الشيخ عن الدعوة إلى الله تعالى وضوابطها، ثم أكد أن هدف الدعوة إلى الله تعالى هو إقامة الحق والعدل بين الناس، وهو ما تحققه الشريعة الإسلامية حينما تطبق، وذكر فضيلته أن واجب الحاكم هو الحكم بالعدل بين الناس، وأن قضية توليته وعزله من حق عامة الناس، وأن عليه أن يؤدي لكل ذي حق حقه، ويوفر لأفراد الأمة ظروف العيش في جو من الأمن يلبي حاجياتهم ويستجيب لطموحاتهم حتى يبرأ من تبعات حقوقهم. وقد قال الشيخ إن الأمة لا يهمها شخص من يحكمها بقدر ما يهمها الإصلاح، فمن أراد الخير من الحكام وفقه الله له وأعانه على ذلك ببطانة صالحة، مؤكدا أن السلطان سوق يجلب إليه الرائج فيه، ومن قرب بطانة السوء من الحكام فسيجد غب ذلك وسوءاته. كما ذكر سماحة العلامة أن الشعوب الإسلامية لن تظل مكتوفة الأيدي أمام استخفاف الحكام بالشريعة الإسلامية، وعدم تطبيقها، بل الشعوب واجب عليها أن تبذل في سبيل التمكين للدين ورعاية مصالح المسلمين وإنصاف غير المسلمين، وقد رد على بعض الفقهاء الذين يكيفون أحكام الخليفة على حكام بلاد المسلمين اليوم، حيث إن هؤلاء الحكام لم يدعوا أنهم يسعون لتطبيق الشريعة ولا أنهم خلفاء عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في إقامة الدين وسياسة الدنيا به، بل هم أقرب يضيف فضيلة الشيخ إلى حكام الأمصار في عهد الخلافة الراشدة. وأفاد فضيلة الشيخ أن آلية اختيار الخليفة المسلم ظلت خاضعة للظروف، مقارنا بين طريقة اختيار أبي بكر وعمر وعثمان وعلي، وأن الخليفة الذي وعدت به الأحاديث الشريفة ستكون آلية اختياره حسبما هو معروف في زمانه. محاضرة هامة تطرقت لنقاط كثيرة، للمتابعة على الموقع اضغط هنا: للمتابعة بدقة عالية اضغط هنا:
body_en:
On the evening of yesterday, Tuesday 4 Jumada al-Ula 1433 AH, corresponding to 27 March 2012, the Cultural Diversity Space hosted an important scholarly lecture organised by the Future Association under the title "Say: This is my way". The lecture was delivered by Sheikh Muhammad al-Hasan Ould al-Dedew, president of the Centre for the Formation of Scholars and president of the Future Association for Calling to Islam, Culture and Education, amid a heavy public turnout that filled the precincts of the wide space to overflowing.

At the outset of his talk the Sheikh spoke about calling people to God Most High (daʿwah) and its governing conditions; he then affirmed that the aim of calling people to God Most High is the establishment of truth and of justice among people, which is what Islamic law achieves when it is applied. He mentioned that the ruler's obligation (wājib) is to judge with justice among the people; that the question of his being given office and of his removal from it belongs by right to the general body of the people; and that he must render to every holder of a right his right, and must provide the members of the community with conditions of life in an atmosphere of security that meets their needs and answers to their aspirations, so that he may be discharged of the liabilities attaching to their rights.

The Sheikh said that the community is not concerned with the person of whoever rules it so much as it is concerned with reform; that whichever of the rulers desires good, God grants him success in it and aids him in it with a righteous inner circle; and he affirmed that authority is a marketplace, to which is brought whatever sells well in it, and that whoever brings an inner circle of evil men close among the rulers will find the outcome of that and its ills.

The eminent scholar also mentioned that the Muslim peoples will not remain with their hands folded before the rulers' making light of Islamic law and their failure to apply it; rather it is obligatory (wājib) upon the peoples to expend effort towards the establishing of the religion, the safeguarding of the interests of the Muslims and the doing of justice to non-Muslims. He answered some jurists who fit the rulings pertaining to the caliph onto the rulers of the Muslim lands today, on the ground that these rulers have not claimed that they seek to apply Islamic law, nor that they are successors to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in establishing the religion and in governing worldly affairs by it; rather — the Sheikh adds — they are closer to the governors of the provinces in the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphate.

The Sheikh stated that the mechanism for choosing the Muslim caliph has remained subject to circumstances, comparing the manner in which Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali were chosen; and that the caliph promised in the noble hadiths will have his mechanism of selection according to whatever is recognised in his own time.

An important lecture, which addressed many points.

flags.arabic: وأن قضية توليته وعزله من حق عامة الناس ... بل الشعوب واجب عليها أن تبذل في سبيل التمكين للدين
flags.context: the report's account of the Sheikh's position on rulers and on the duty of the peoples
options: translate faithfully and refer the publication decision upward
translate and publish as ordinary content
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW, style guide section 12, and the most consequential record in this slice. As summarised, the Sheikh is made to hold that the appointment AND removal of a ruler is the right of the general body of the people; that today's rulers of Muslim states are not caliphs and that the jurists who treat them as such are wrong; and that it is obligatory (wājib) upon the peoples not to stay passive. In March 2012, in Mauritania, in Arabic, addressed to that audience, this is one thing; the same sentences under his name in English, indexed and quotable, are another, and could carry legal consequence for him in several jurisdictions. Nothing has been softened, strengthened or qualified. Crucially, this is a news desk's compression, not a transcript: every qualification the Sheikh may have attached is absent by construction. The decision whether and how to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.arabic: واجب الحاكم هو الحكم بالعدل ... بل الشعوب واجب عليها أن تبذل
flags.context: the ruling word wājib, used twice of political conduct
flags.note: The fixed mapping is applied: wājib is 'obligatory' and never 'must', 'should' or 'required' alone. But note what is being graded. These are the news desk's words reporting the Sheikh, not his own wording, and a legal grading carried across in a summary is exactly the kind of thing the five-rulings table exists to protect. The English preserves the grading and its strength; it does not warrant that the Sheikh used the word wājib, and the record gives no evidence either way. Note also that the first wājib grades the conduct of the ruler and the second the conduct of whole peoples — a far stronger claim, and the one that matters.

flags.arabic: السلطان سوق يجلب إليه الرائج فيه
flags.context: quoted by the Sheikh without attribution, as the news desk has it
options: authority is a marketplace, to which is brought whatever sells well in it
power is a market: what is in demand there is what is supplied
the ruler is a market to which people bring what finds a buyer
flags.note: A proverb of the early caliphate, most often attributed to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and preserved in the adab literature, here quoted with no attribution — whether by the Sheikh or by the reporter cannot be told. The image is that courtiers supply whatever the ruler is known to want, so a ruler's character determines the character of those around him. The English keeps the metaphor rather than explaining it, since explaining it would add reasoning the record does not contain.

flags.arabic: الخليفة الذي وعدت به الأحاديث الشريفة
flags.context: the closing sentence on the mechanism for choosing a caliph
options: render exactly, with the hadiths unnamed as the source leaves them
flags.note: The report refers to 'the caliph promised in the noble hadiths' and names no report, gives no collection and no grading. Style guide section 4 forbids adding a grading the Sheikh did not give and dropping one he did; here there is none to carry, so nothing has been supplied. The referent is presumably the awaited caliph of the end-time reports, but the corpus cannot establish that from a summary.

flags.context: the association's name, against records 781 and 783
options: render each occurrence as the source gives it
flags.note: The same body is called 'the Future Association for Upbringing, Culture and Education' in records 781 and 783 and 'for Calling to Islam, Culture and Education' here. The variation is the source's and has not been harmonised. A reviewer should establish the registered name before the English fixes one.

translator_notes: A news-desk report, not a transcript. Every position attributed to the Sheikh here arrives compressed and at second hand, and the record itself ends by pointing to two recordings that the corpus does not hold.
The CMS timestamp, 28 March 2012, is a bulk-upload date; the body dates the lecture to the evening of Tuesday 4 Jumada al-Ula 1433 / 27 March 2012.

'قل هذه سبيلي' is Sūrat Yūsuf 12:108, used here as a lecture title. The source gives it in ordinary quotation marks with no reference, and the English keeps it that way rather than applying the curly-brace citation convention to a title.

'ضوابط' is rendered 'governing conditions' and deliberately not as شرط/'condition' from the glossary, which is a technical fiqh term for a condition of validity; ḍawābiṭ here are the controls or constraints proper to the activity of daʿwah.
